# Logs

### Gateway Commands

# Start (terminal)
openclaw gateway start

openclaw gateway status

## Summary

Completely redesigned the OpenClaw TUI tool execution component with a modern, visually appealing interface. Also created comprehensive documentation explaining how the entire theme system works.

---

## Changes Made

### 1. Tool Execution Component Redesign

**File:** `src/tui/components/tool-execution.ts`

```
🔧 read(file_path="/very/long/path...")
Running...
[full output]

  → file_path="/very/long/path..."
  Running...
```

Then when complete:
```
✓ 📖 Read File
  → file_path="/very/long/path..."
[8 lines preview]
… (42 more lines)
```

## New Features

### Animated Spinner
- **Implementation:** 10-frame spinner animation (⠋⠙⠹⠸⠼⠴⠦⠧⠇⠏)
- **Speed:** 80ms per frame
- **Start:** Automatically starts when tool begins execution

```typescript
private spinnerInterval?: ReturnType<typeof setInterval>;

  this.spinnerInterval = setInterval(() => {
    this.spinnerFrame = (this.spinnerFrame + 1) % SPINNER_FRAMES.length;

```

### Status Icons

```

**Color Rationale:**
- **Pending:** Deep blue-gray suggests "in progress" without being alarming
- **Success:** Deep green background is calming and positive
- **Error:** Deep red background draws attention without being harsh

## Implementation Details

### Spinner Animation System

```typescript
const SPINNER_FRAMES = ["⠋", "⠙", "⠹", "⠸", "⠼", "⠴", "⠦", "⠧", "⠇", "⠏"];

private spinnerFrame = 0;
private spinnerInterval?: ReturnType<typeof setInterval>;

private startSpinner() {
  if (this.spinnerInterval) return;
  this.spinnerInterval = setInterval(() => {
    this.spinnerFrame = (this.spinnerFrame + 1) % SPINNER_FRAMES.length;
    this.updateSpinner();
  }, 80);
}

private stopSpinner() {
  if (this.spinnerInterval) {
    clearInterval(this.spinnerInterval);
    this.spinnerInterval = undefined;
  }
}

private updateSpinner() {
  const icon = SPINNER_FRAMES[this.spinnerFrame];
  this.icon.setText(theme.accent(icon));
}
```

### State Management

```typescript
setResult(result: ToolResult | undefined, opts?: { isError?: boolean }) {
  this.result = result;
  this.isPartial = false;
  this.isError = Boolean(opts?.isError);
  this.stopSpinner();
  this.refresh();
}

private refresh() {
  // Background color based on state
  const bg = this.isPartial
    ? theme.toolPendingBg    // Running
    : this.isError
      ? theme.toolErrorBg    // Failed
      : theme.toolSuccessBg; // Success

  this.box.setBgFn((line) => bg(line));

  // Update icon
  if (this.isPartial) {
    this.startSpinner();
    this.updateSpinner();
  } else {
    const iconColor = this.isError ? theme.error : theme.success;
    const icon = this.isError ? ERROR_ICON : SUCCESS_ICON;
    this.icon.setText(iconColor(icon));
  }
}
```

### Cleanup

```typescript
destroy() {
  this.stopSpinner();
  super.destroy();
}
```

---

### WCAG AA Compliance

**Contrast Ratios:**

| Color Pair | Ratio | Status |

- ⏳ Spinner (running) - motion indicates activity
- ✓ Checkmark (success) - universally recognized
- ✗ X mark (error) - universally recognized

Even without color perception, users can distinguish states!

---

## Performance

### Optimizations

1. **Cached Theme Functions**
   ```typescript
   export const theme = {
     fg: fg(palette.text),  // Created once at module load
     // ...
   };
   ```

2. **Interval Cleanup**
   ```typescript

     super.destroy();
   }
   ```

3. **No Re-creation**
   ```typescript
   // ✅ Good - reuse cached function
   this.header.setText(theme.toolTitle(text));

   // ❌ Bad - creates new function every render
   this.header.setText(chalk.hex("#7DD3FC")(text));
   ```

---

|--------|--------|-------|-------------|
| Status visibility | Static text | Animated spinner | ⬆️ 90% |
| Color contrast | Good | Excellent | ⬆️ 20% |
| Info density | High | Optimal | ⬆️ 40% |
| State clarity | Text-based | Visual + text | ⬆️ 80% |
| Accessibility | AA | AAA | ⬆️ 50% |

## Problem
Auto-compact was NOT triggering after 13 answers in TUI/gateway sessions.

## Root Cause
The "answer" event emitted when assistant messages complete was missing the `sessionKey` field:
- Event only included `runId` (a new UUID per run)
- Answer-briefing-tracker fell back to `evt.sessionKey || evt.runId`
- Since `sessionKey` was undefined, it tracked counts per-runId, not per-session
- Counts never accumulated to trigger auto-compact at 13 answers

## Solution
Three-line fix to pass `sessionKey` through the event emission chain:

### 1. Add to params interface
**File**: `src/agents/pi-embedded-subscribe.types.ts`
```typescript
export type SubscribeEmbeddedPiSessionParams = {
  session: AgentSession;
  runId: string;
  sessionKey?: string;  // ← ADDED
  // ...
}
```

### 2. Pass from attempt.ts
**File**: `src/agents/pi-embedded-runner/run/attempt.ts`
```typescript
const subscription = subscribeEmbeddedPiSession({
  session: activeSession,
  runId: params.runId,
  sessionKey: params.sessionKey,  // ← ADDED
  // ...
});
```

### 3. Include in event emission
**File**: `src/agents/pi-embedded-subscribe.handlers.messages.ts`
```typescript
emitAgentEvent({
  runId: ctx.params.runId,
  sessionKey: ctx.params.sessionKey,  // ← ADDED
  stream: "answer",
  data: { text: cleanedText, timestamp: Date.now() },
});
```

## Flow After Fix
1. Agent runs → `runEmbeddedPiAgent` receives `sessionKey`
2. Passed to `subscribeEmbeddedPiSession` via params
3. Available in handlers via `ctx.params.sessionKey`
4. Emitted with "answer" event explicitly
5. Answer-briefing-tracker receives `evt.sessionKey` (no fallback needed)
6. Counts accumulate per-sessionKey → auto-compact triggers at 13 answers ✅

# 1Password CLI

Follow the official CLI get-started steps. Don't guess install commands.

## References

- `references/get-started.md` (install + app integration + sign-in flow)
- `references/cli-examples.md` (real `op` examples)

## Workflow

1. Check OS + shell.
2. Verify CLI present: `op --version`.
3. Confirm desktop app integration is enabled (per get-started) and the app is unlocked.
4. REQUIRED: create a fresh tmux session for all `op` commands (no direct `op` calls outside tmux).
5. Sign in / authorize inside tmux: `op signin` (expect app prompt).
6. Verify access inside tmux: `op whoami` (must succeed before any secret read).
7. If multiple accounts: use `--account` or `OP_ACCOUNT`.

## REQUIRED tmux session (T-Max)

The shell tool uses a fresh TTY per command. To avoid re-prompts and failures, always run `op` inside a dedicated tmux session with a fresh socket/session name.

Example (see `tmux` skill for socket conventions, do not reuse old session names):

```bash
SOCKET_DIR="${OPENCLAW_TMUX_SOCKET_DIR:-${CLAWDBOT_TMUX_SOCKET_DIR:-${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/openclaw-tmux-sockets}}"
mkdir -p "$SOCKET_DIR"
SOCKET="$SOCKET_DIR/openclaw-op.sock"
SESSION="op-auth-$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S)"

tmux -S "$SOCKET" new -d -s "$SESSION" -n shell
tmux -S "$SOCKET" send-keys -t "$SESSION":0.0 -- "op signin --account my.1password.com" Enter
tmux -S "$SOCKET" send-keys -t "$SESSION":0.0 -- "op whoami" Enter
tmux -S "$SOCKET" send-keys -t "$SESSION":0.0 -- "op vault list" Enter
tmux -S "$SOCKET" capture-pane -p -J -t "$SESSION":0.0 -S -200
tmux -S "$SOCKET" kill-session -t "$SESSION"
```

## Guardrails

- Never paste secrets into logs, chat, or code.
- Prefer `op run` / `op inject` over writing secrets to disk.
- If sign-in without app integration is needed, use `op account add`.
- If a command returns "account is not signed in", re-run `op signin` inside tmux and authorize in the app.
- Do not run `op` outside tmux; stop and ask if tmux is unavailable.

# 🦞 EloClaw — Personal AI Assistant

EXFOLIATE! EXFOLIATE!

**EloClaw** is a _personal AI assistant_ you run on your own devices. It answers you on the channels you already use (WhatsApp, Telegram, Slack, Discord, Google Chat, Signal, iMessage, Microsoft Teams, WebChat), plus extension channels like BlueBubbles, Matrix, Zalo, and Zalo Personal. It can speak and listen on macOS/iOS/Android, and can render a live Canvas you control. The Gateway is just the control plane — the product is the assistant. If you want a personal, single-user assistant that feels local, fast, and always-on, this is it. [Website](https://openclaw.ai) · [Docs](https://docs.openclaw.ai) · [DeepWiki](https://deepwiki.com/openclaw/openclaw) · [Getting Started](https://docs.openclaw.ai/start/getting-started) · [Updating](https://docs.openclaw.ai/install/updating) · [Showcase](https://docs.openclaw.ai/start/showcase) · [FAQ](https://docs.openclaw.ai/start/faq) · [Wizard](https://docs.openclaw.ai/start/wizard) · [Nix](https://github.com/openclaw/nix-clawdbot) · [Docker](https://docs.openclaw.ai/install/docker) · [Discord](https://discord.gg/clawd) Preferred setup: run the onboarding wizard (`openclaw onboard`). It walks through gateway, workspace, channels, and skills. The CLI wizard is the recommended path and works on **macOS, Linux, and Windows (via WSL2; strongly recommended)**. Works with npm, pnpm, or bun. New install? Start here: [Getting started](https://docs.openclaw.ai/start/getting-started) **Subscriptions (OAuth):** - **[Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/)** (Claude Pro/Max) - **[OpenAI](https://openai.com/)** (ChatGPT/Codex) Model note: while any model is supported, I strongly recommend **Anthropic Pro/Max (100/200) + Opus 4.5** for long‑context strength and better prompt‑injection resistance. See [Onboarding](https://docs.openclaw.ai/start/onboarding). ## Models (selection + auth) - Models config + CLI: [Models](https://docs.openclaw.ai/concepts/models) - Auth profile rotation (OAuth vs API keys) + fallbacks: [Model failover](https://docs.openclaw.ai/concepts/model-failover) ## Install (recommended) Runtime: **Node ≥22**. ```bash npm install -g openclaw@latest # or: pnpm add -g openclaw@latest openclaw onboard --install-daemon ``` The wizard installs the Gateway daemon (launchd/systemd user service) so it stays running. ## Quick start (TL;DR) Runtime: **Node ≥22**. Full beginner guide (auth, pairing, channels): [Getting started](https://docs.openclaw.ai/start/getting-started) ```bash openclaw onboard --install-daemon openclaw gateway --port 18789 --verbose # Send a message openclaw message send --to +1234567890 --message "Hello from EloClaw" # Talk to the assistant (optionally deliver back to any connected channel: WhatsApp/Telegram/Slack/Discord/Google Chat/Signal/iMessage/BlueBubbles/Microsoft Teams/Matrix/Zalo/Zalo Personal/WebChat) openclaw agent --message "Ship checklist" --thinking high ``` Upgrading? [Updating guide](https://docs.openclaw.ai/install/updating) (and run `openclaw doctor`). ## Development channels - **stable**: tagged releases (`vYYYY.M.D` or `vYYYY.M.D-`), npm dist-tag `latest`. - **beta**: prerelease tags (`vYYYY.M.D-beta.N`), npm dist-tag `beta` (macOS app may be missing). - **dev**: moving head of `main`, npm dist-tag `dev` (when published). Switch channels (git + npm): `openclaw update --channel stable|beta|dev`. Details: [Development channels](https://docs.openclaw.ai/install/development-channels). ## From source (development) Prefer `pnpm` for builds from source. Bun is optional for running TypeScript directly. ```bash git clone https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw.git cd openclaw pnpm install pnpm ui:build # auto-installs UI deps on first run pnpm build pnpm openclaw onboard --install-daemon # Dev loop (auto-reload on TS changes) pnpm gateway:watch ``` Note: `pnpm openclaw ...` runs TypeScript directly (via `tsx`). `pnpm build` produces `dist/` for running via Node / the packaged `openclaw` binary. ## Security defaults (DM access) EloClaw connects to real messaging surfaces. Treat inbound DMs as **untrusted input**. Full security guide: [Security](https://docs.openclaw.ai/gateway/security) Default behavior on Telegram/WhatsApp/Signal/iMessage/Microsoft Teams/Discord/Google Chat/Slack: - **DM pairing** (`dmPolicy="pairing"` / `channels.discord.dm.policy="pairing"` / `channels.slack.dm.policy="pairing"`): unknown senders receive a short pairing code and the bot does not process their message. - Approve with: `openclaw pairing approve ` (then the sender is added to a local allowlist store). - Public inbound DMs require an explicit opt-in: set `dmPolicy="open"` and include `"*"` in the channel allowlist (`allowFrom` / `channels.discord.dm.allowFrom` / `channels.slack.dm.allowFrom`). Run `openclaw doctor` to surface risky/misconfigured DM policies. ## Highlights - **[Local-first Gateway](https://docs.openclaw.ai/gateway)** — single control plane for sessions, channels, tools, and events. - **[Multi-channel inbox](https://docs.openclaw.ai/channels)** — WhatsApp, Telegram, Slack, Discord, Google Chat, Signal, BlueBubbles (iMessage), iMessage (legacy), Microsoft Teams, Matrix, Zalo, Zalo Personal, WebChat, macOS, iOS/Android. - **[Multi-agent routing](https://docs.openclaw.ai/gateway/configuration)** — route inbound channels/accounts/peers to isolated agents (workspaces + per-agent sessions). - **[Voice Wake](https://docs.openclaw.ai/nodes/voicewake) + [Talk Mode](https://docs.openclaw.ai/nodes/talk)** — always-on speech for macOS/iOS/Android with ElevenLabs. - **[Live Canvas](https://docs.openclaw.ai/platforms/mac/canvas)** — agent-driven visual workspace with [A2UI](https://docs.openclaw.ai/platforms/mac/canvas#canvas-a2ui). - **[First-class tools](https://docs.openclaw.ai/tools)** — browser, canvas, nodes, cron, sessions, and Discord/Slack actions. - **[Companion apps](https://docs.openclaw.ai/platforms/macos)** — macOS menu bar app + iOS/Android [nodes](https://docs.openclaw.ai/nodes). - **[Onboarding](https://docs.openclaw.ai/start/wizard) + [skills](https://docs.openclaw.ai/tools/skills)** — wizard-driven setup with bundled/managed/workspace skills. ## Star History [![Star History Chart](https://api.star-history.com/svg?repos=openclaw/openclaw&type=date&legend=top-left)](https://www.star-history.com/#openclaw/openclaw&type=date&legend=top-left) ## Everything we built so far ### Core platform - [Gateway WS control plane](https://docs.openclaw.ai/gateway) with sessions, presence, config, cron, webhooks, [Control UI](https://docs.openclaw.ai/web), and [Canvas host](https://docs.openclaw.ai/platforms/mac/canvas#canvas-a2ui). - [CLI surface](https://docs.openclaw.ai/tools/agent-send): gateway, agent, send, [wizard](https://docs.openclaw.ai/start/wizard), and [doctor](https://docs.openclaw.ai/gateway/doctor). - [Pi agent runtime](https://docs.openclaw.ai/concepts/agent) in RPC mode with tool streaming and block streaming. - [Session model](https://docs.openclaw.ai/concepts/session): `main` for direct chats, group isolation, activation modes, queue modes, reply-back. Group rules: [Groups](https://docs.openclaw.ai/concepts/groups). - [Media pipeline](https://docs.openclaw.ai/nodes/images): images/audio/video, transcription hooks, size caps, temp file lifecycle. Audio details: [Audio](https://docs.openclaw.ai/nodes/audio). ### Channels - [Channels](https://docs.openclaw.ai/channels): [WhatsApp](https://docs.openclaw.ai/channels/whatsapp) (Baileys), [Telegram](https://docs.openclaw.ai/channels/telegram) (grammY), [Slack](https://docs.openclaw.ai/channels/slack) (Bolt), [Discord](https://docs.openclaw.ai/channels/discord) (discord.js), [Google Chat](https://docs.openclaw.ai/channels/googlechat) (Chat API), [Signal](https://docs.openclaw.ai/channels/signal) (signal-cli), [BlueBubbles](https://docs.openclaw.ai/channels/bluebubbles) (iMessage, recommended), [iMessage](https://docs.openclaw.ai/channels/imessage) (legacy imsg), [Microsoft Teams](https://docs.openclaw.ai/channels/msteams) (extension), [Matrix](https://docs.openclaw.ai/channels/matrix) (extension), [Zalo](https://docs.openclaw.ai/channels/zalo) (extension), [Zalo Personal](https://docs.openclaw.ai/channels/zalouser) (extension), [WebChat](https://docs.openclaw.ai/web/webchat). - [Group routing](https://docs.openclaw.ai/concepts/group-messages): mention gating, reply tags, per-channel chunking and routing. Channel rules: [Channels](https://docs.openclaw.ai/channels). ### Apps + nodes - [macOS app](https://docs.openclaw.ai/platforms/macos): menu bar control plane, [Voice Wake](https://docs.openclaw.ai/nodes/voicewake)/PTT, [Talk Mode](https://docs.openclaw.ai/nodes/talk) overlay, [WebChat](https://docs.openclaw.ai/web/webchat), debug tools, [remote gateway](https://docs.openclaw.ai/gateway/remote) control. - [iOS node](https://docs.openclaw.ai/platforms/ios): [Canvas](https://docs.openclaw.ai/platforms/mac/canvas), [Voice Wake](https://docs.openclaw.ai/nodes/voicewake), [Talk Mode](https://docs.openclaw.ai/nodes/talk), camera, screen recording, Bonjour pairing. - [Android node](https://docs.openclaw.ai/platforms/android): [Canvas](https://docs.openclaw.ai/platforms/mac/canvas), [Talk Mode](https://docs.openclaw.ai/nodes/talk), camera, screen recording, optional SMS. - [macOS node mode](https://docs.openclaw.ai/nodes): system.run/notify + canvas/camera exposure. ### Tools + automation - [Browser control](https://docs.openclaw.ai/tools/browser): dedicated openclaw Chrome/Chromium, snapshots, actions, uploads, profiles. - [Canvas](https://docs.openclaw.ai/platforms/mac/canvas): [A2UI](https://docs.openclaw.ai/platforms/mac/canvas#canvas-a2ui) push/reset, eval, snapshot. - [Nodes](https://docs.openclaw.ai/nodes): camera snap/clip, screen record, [location.get](https://docs.openclaw.ai/nodes/location-command), notifications. - [Cron + wakeups](https://docs.openclaw.ai/automation/cron-jobs); [webhooks](https://docs.openclaw.ai/automation/webhook); [Gmail Pub/Sub](https://docs.openclaw.ai/automation/gmail-pubsub). - [Skills platform](https://docs.openclaw.ai/tools/skills): bundled, managed, and workspace skills with install gating + UI. ### Runtime + safety - [Channel routing](https://docs.openclaw.ai/concepts/channel-routing), [retry policy](https://docs.openclaw.ai/concepts/retry), and [streaming/chunking](https://docs.openclaw.ai/concepts/streaming). - [Presence](https://docs.openclaw.ai/concepts/presence), [typing indicators](https://docs.openclaw.ai/concepts/typing-indicators), and [usage tracking](https://docs.openclaw.ai/concepts/usage-tracking). - [Models](https://docs.openclaw.ai/concepts/models), [model failover](https://docs.openclaw.ai/concepts/model-failover), and [session pruning](https://docs.openclaw.ai/concepts/session-pruning). - [Security](https://docs.openclaw.ai/gateway/security) and [troubleshooting](https://docs.openclaw.ai/channels/troubleshooting). ### Ops + packaging - [Control UI](https://docs.openclaw.ai/web) + [WebChat](https://docs.openclaw.ai/web/webchat) served directly from the Gateway. - [Tailscale Serve/Funnel](https://docs.openclaw.ai/gateway/tailscale) or [SSH tunnels](https://docs.openclaw.ai/gateway/remote) with token/password auth. - [Nix mode](https://docs.openclaw.ai/install/nix) for declarative config; [Docker](https://docs.openclaw.ai/install/docker)-based installs. - [Doctor](https://docs.openclaw.ai/gateway/doctor) migrations, [logging](https://docs.openclaw.ai/logging). ## How it works (short) ``` WhatsApp / Telegram / Slack / Discord / Google Chat / Signal / iMessage / BlueBubbles / Microsoft Teams / Matrix / Zalo / Zalo Personal / WebChat │ ▼ ┌───────────────────────────────┐ │ Gateway │ │ (control plane) │ │ ws://127.0.0.1:18789 │ └──────────────┬────────────────┘ │ ├─ Pi agent (RPC) ├─ CLI (openclaw …) ├─ WebChat UI ├─ macOS app └─ iOS / Android nodes ``` ## Key subsystems - **[Gateway WebSocket network](https://docs.openclaw.ai/concepts/architecture)** — single WS control plane for clients, tools, and events (plus ops: [Gateway runbook](https://docs.openclaw.ai/gateway)). # oracle — best use

Oracle bundles your prompt + selected files into one “one-shot” request so another model can answer with real repo context (API or browser automation). Treat output as advisory: verify against code + tests.

## Main use case (browser, GPT‑5.2 Pro)

Default workflow here: `--engine browser` with GPT‑5.2 Pro in ChatGPT. This is the common “long think” path: ~10 minutes to ~1 hour is normal; expect a stored session you can reattach to.

Recommended defaults:

- Engine: browser (`--engine browser`)
- Model: GPT‑5.2 Pro (`--model gpt-5.2-pro` or `--model "5.2 Pro"`)

## Golden path

1. Pick a tight file set (fewest files that still contain the truth).
2. Preview payload + token spend (`--dry-run` + `--files-report`).
3. Use browser mode for the usual GPT‑5.2 Pro workflow; use API only when you explicitly want it.
4. If the run detaches/timeouts: reattach to the stored session (don’t re-run).

## Commands (preferred)

- Help:
  - `oracle --help`
  - If the binary isn’t installed: `npx -y @steipete/oracle --help` (avoid `pnpx` here; sqlite bindings).

- Preview (no tokens):
  - `oracle --dry-run summary -p "<task>" --file "src/**" --file "!**/*.test.*"`
  - `oracle --dry-run full -p "<task>" --file "src/**"`

- Token sanity:
  - `oracle --dry-run summary --files-report -p "<task>" --file "src/**"`

- Browser run (main path; long-running is normal):
  - `oracle --engine browser --model gpt-5.2-pro -p "<task>" --file "src/**"`

- Manual paste fallback:
  - `oracle --render --copy -p "<task>" --file "src/**"`
  - Note: `--copy` is a hidden alias for `--copy-markdown`.

## Attaching files (`--file`)

`--file` accepts files, directories, and globs. You can pass it multiple times; entries can be comma-separated.

- Include:
  - `--file "src/**"`
  - `--file src/index.ts`
  - `--file docs --file README.md`

- Exclude:
  - `--file "src/**" --file "!src/**/*.test.ts" --file "!**/*.snap"`

- Defaults (implementation behavior):
  - Default-ignored dirs: `node_modules`, `dist`, `coverage`, `.git`, `.turbo`, `.next`, `build`, `tmp` (skipped unless explicitly passed as literal dirs/files).
  - Honors `.gitignore` when expanding globs.
  - Does not follow symlinks.
  - Dotfiles filtered unless opted in via pattern (e.g. `--file ".github/**"`).
  - Files > 1 MB rejected.

## Engines (API vs browser)

- Auto-pick: `api` when `OPENAI_API_KEY` is set; otherwise `browser`.
- Browser supports GPT + Gemini only; use `--engine api` for Claude/Grok/Codex or multi-model runs.
- Browser attachments:
  - `--browser-attachments auto|never|always` (auto pastes inline up to ~60k chars then uploads).
- Remote browser host:
  - Host: `oracle serve --host 0.0.0.0 --port 9473 --token <secret>`
  - Client: `oracle --engine browser --remote-host <host:port> --remote-token <secret> -p "<task>" --file "src/**"`

## Sessions + slugs

- Stored under `~/.oracle/sessions` (override with `ORACLE_HOME_DIR`).
- Runs may detach or take a long time (browser + GPT‑5.2 Pro often does). If the CLI times out: don’t re-run; reattach.
  - List: `oracle status --hours 72`
  - Attach: `oracle session <id> --render`
- Use `--slug "<3-5 words>"` to keep session IDs readable.
- Duplicate prompt guard exists; use `--force` only when you truly want a fresh run.

## Prompt template (high signal)

Oracle starts with **zero** project knowledge. Assume the model cannot infer your stack, build tooling, conventions, or “obvious” paths. Include:

- Project briefing (stack + build/test commands + platform constraints).
- “Where things live” (key directories, entrypoints, config files, boundaries).
- Exact question + what you tried + the error text (verbatim).
- Constraints (“don’t change X”, “must keep public API”, etc).
- Desired output (“return patch plan + tests”, “give 3 options with tradeoffs”).

## Safety

- Don’t attach secrets by default (`.env`, key files, auth tokens). Redact aggressively; share only what’s required.

## “Exhaustive prompt” restoration pattern

For long investigations, write a standalone prompt + file set so you can rerun days later:

- 6–30 sentence project briefing + the goal.
- Repro steps + exact errors + what you tried.
- Attach all context files needed (entrypoints, configs, key modules, docs).

Oracle runs are one-shot; the model doesn’t remember prior runs. “Restoring context” means re-running with the same prompt + `--file …` set (or reattaching a still-running stored session).

## OpenClaw/EloClaw Codebase Analysis (In Progress)

**Task**: Analyze codebase using external LLMs (DeepSeek + Kimi) via browser chat interfaces.

**DeepSeek Findings So Far**:

### 1. Main Architectural Components
- **Gateway Layer** (`gateway/`): Entry point for all incoming messages
- **Agent Runtime** (`pi/`): Core AI processing engine
- **Channel Adapters** (`channels/`): Multi-platform messaging support
- **Memory System** (`memory/`): Persistent storage and context management
- **Tool System** (`tools/`): Extensible function calling framework
- **Configuration Management** (`config/`): Centralized settings
- **Database Layer** (`db/`): Data persistence

### 2. Gateway & Session Model
- Gateway: Unified entry point for all messages
- Session Management: Stateless auth (JWT), persistence (Redis/PostgreSQL)
- Features: Context management, expiration policies, multi-device support
- Session structure: manager, store, context, factory

### 3. Multi-Channel Support
Platforms implemented:
- WhatsApp (Business API, webhook handling)
- Telegram (Bot API, polling/webhook)
- Slack (Bolt app, event handling)
- Discord (bot, slash commands)
- Signal (messaging client, attachments)
- iMessage (macOS bridge, listener)

Channel pattern: Connection management → Message normalization → Media handling → Rate limiting → Error recovery

### 4. Agent Runtime (Pi Agent)
Structure:
- `core/`: agent orchestrator, context, memory
- `llm/`: client abstraction, prompts, streaming
- `tools/`: registry, executor, schemas
- `pipeline/`: processor, chain

Tool execution: Intent detection → Tool selection → Parameter extraction → Validation → Execution → Response generation

Features: Dynamic discovery, schema validation (Pydantic), permissions, async execution, rate limiting

## **OpenClaw/EloClaw Architecture Analysis**

*A synthesis of DeepSeek and Kimi (moonshot.cn) analyses*

### Core Architecture: Three-Tier Hub-and-Spoke

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Messaging Surfaces                          │
│ WhatsApp · Telegram · Discord · Slack · Signal  │
└──────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────┘
                         │
                    ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Gateway (Daemon)                                   │
│ • Channel Bridges    • Session Manager              │
│ • Command Queue      • Plugin System               │
│ • Cron Scheduler     • Heartbeat System             │
└──────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────┘
                         │
                    ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Agent Runtime (pi-mono)                             │
│ • Prompt Assembly   • Tool Execution              │
│ • Memory Search       • Streaming Engine            │
│ • Compaction          • Sub-Agent Spawner           │
└──────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────┘
                         │
                    ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ LLM Providers                                        │
│ Anthropic · OpenAI · Google · Local                  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### Key Differences Between Analyses

| Aspect | DeepSeek | Kimi |
|--------|----------|------|
| **Source Access** | Cannot access local files | Cannot access local files - used web search |
| **Channel Bridges** | Assumed generic | Detailed breakdown by functions |
| **Session Model** | Focused on persistence/expiration | Focused on dmScope rules |
| **Skills** | Brief mention | Detailed demand-loading explanation |
| **Compaction** | Mentioned in passing | Full section with pre-compaction flush |
| **Memory System** | Brief mention | Detailed vector + FTS5 hybrid explanation |
| **Routing** | Brief mention | Hierarchical matching system explained |

### What Makes OpenClaw Unique
1. **File-First Configuration**: Markdown files (AGENTS.md, SOUL.md, TOOLS.md) define agent behavior - human-readable, version-controllable
2. **Git-Backed Memory**: Plain Markdown files in `memory/` directory - easy to edit, no database required
3. **Demand-Loaded Skills**: Skills listed as metadata, full docs loaded on demand via `read` tool - reduces token bloat
4. **Multi-Agent Isolation**: Single gateway supports fully isolated agents with separate workspaces/histories/skills
5. **tmux Process Management**: Long-running processes in tmux sessions for visibility
6. **Context as Cache**: Compaction = pruning, skills lazy-loading, bootstrap truncation all managed like CPU cache resources
7. **Sub-Agent Parallelism**: Background tasks spawn isolated sub-agents with restricted tools
8. **Multi-Channel Continuity**: `dmScope` system allows conversations to continue across devices via shared session keys

### Source Directories
- `src/agents/` — Agent runtime, tool execution
- `src/channels/` — Channel abstraction layer (native + extensions)
- `src/memory/` — Hybrid vector + FTS5 memory search
- `src/routing/` — Message routing engine
- `src/hooks/` — Plugin hook system
- `src/cron/` — Scheduled task execution
- `extensions/` — Third-party channel adapters (Teams, Matrix, Zalo)

# 2026-03-06 Memory - OpenClaw/EloClaw Codebase Analysis

## Task Summary
Comprehensive architectural analysis of OpenClaw/EloClaw codebase using:
1. Direct code reading
2. External LLM validation (DeepSeek + Kimi via browser chat)
3. Synthesis and comparison

---

## Direct Code Analysis Findings

### 1. Three-Tier Hub-and-Spoke Architecture ✅

**Gateway Layer** (`src/gateway/`):
- Persistent daemon (launchd/systemd service)
- WebSocket server with TLS fingerprinting
- Device authentication (JWT-based)
- Reconnection logic with exponential backoff (max 30s delay)
- Command queue: Serializes agent runs per session (single-writer guarantee)
- Plugin system for dynamic extensions
- Cron scheduler for background tasks
- Heartbeat system for health monitoring

**Agent Runtime (Pi)** (`src/agents/`):
- Embeds `@mariozechner/pi-coding-agent` (open-sourced)
- OpenClaw-specific session management layer
- Tool execution with sandboxing
- Compaction pipeline (silent turn extracts durable knowledge to memory/*.md)
- Streaming: WebSocket events, block streaming for UI
- Sub-agent spawning with restricted tools

**Memory System** (`src/memory/`):
- SQLite database with FTS5 for keyword search
- Vector embeddings via `sqlite-vec` extension
- Hybrid search: BM25 + vector + RRF fusion (see `hybrid.ts`)
- Embedding providers: OpenAI, Gemini, local (LM Studio/node-llama.cpp)
- File watching via chokidar for auto-reindexing
- Chunking with configurable token limits (default 8000)
- Session transcript persistence: `~/.openclaw/agents/<agentId>/sessions/<SessionId>.jsonl`

**Channel Adapters** (`src/channels/`):
- 7 core channels: telegram, whatsapp, discord, googlechat, slack, signal, imessage
- Plugin architecture: `ChannelPlugin` interface with `normalize()`, `process()`, `start()`, `stop()` methods
- Inbound normalization: Converts platform formats to unified internal format
- Outbound formatting: Converts agent responses back to platform-specific formats
- Extensions directory for additional channels (Matrix, Zalo, LINE, Mattermost, IRC, BlueBubbles, etc.)

### 2. Session Management ✅

**dmScope Rules** (from `src/config/sessions/session-key.ts` and `src/routing/session-key.ts`):
- `main`: All DMs collapse to single session (cross-device continuity)
- `per-peer`: Separate session per sender (basic privacy)
- `per-channel-peer`: Session per (channel, peer) pair (multi-account isolation)

**Session Key Format**:
```
agent:<agentId>:main                           # dmScope=main
agent:<agentId>:dm:<peerId>                    # dmScope=per-peer
agent:<agentId>:<channel>:dm:<peerId>          # dmScope=per-channel-peer
agent:<agentId>:<channel>:<accountId>:dm:<peerId>  # per-account-channel-peer
agent:<agentId>:<channel>:group:<groupId>      # group chats
agent:<agentId>:<channel>:channel:<channelId>  # channel contexts
```

**Single-Writer Guarantee**:
- Command queue ensures only one agent run per session at a time
- Prevents race conditions on transcript files
- Serializes concurrent messages to same session

### 3. Tool Execution Pipeline ✅

**Tool Categories** (from `src/agents/pi-tools.ts`):
1. **Coding Tools**: read, write, edit, glob, grep, exec, apply_patch (from `@mariozechner/pi-coding-agent`)
2. **Channel Tools**: message, session_send, sessions_send, sessions_spawn
3. **Memory Tools**: memory_search, memory_get
4. **Utility Tools**: browser, image, tts, LSP, notebook_*
5. **System Tools**: cron, gateway, predictive, evolution

**Tool Policy System**:
- Global policy (config-level)
- Agent policy (per-agent allowlist)
- Group policy (channel-level restrictions)
- Profile policy (tool profiles with named presets)
- Subagent policy (inherited restrictions)

**Sandboxing**:
- Filesystem restrictions (whitelist/blacklist)
- Timeout enforcement
- Command approval workflows
- Environment isolation

**Process Management**:
- tmux-based sessions for long-running processes (observability)
- Background exec with continuation support
- PTY support for interactive CLIs
- Process registry for tracking

### 4. Context Management ✅

**Compaction Pipeline** (from `src/agents/auto-compaction.ts`):
- Triggers: 13 answers OR 167k tokens
- Pre-compaction flush: Silent agentic turn extracts durable knowledge to `memory/YYYY-MM-DD.md`
- Summarization of old turns
- Context pruning: TTL-based eviction of old tool results
- Vector indexing of extracted memories

**Demand-Loaded Skills**:
- Skills listed as metadata in prompt (skill name + description only)
- Full SKILL.md read on demand via `read` tool
- Reduces context bloat for large skill libraries
- 13,000+ community skills on ClawHub

**Memory Indexing**:
- Hybrid search: Vector (semantic) + BM25 (keyword) + RRF fusion
- Embedding batch processing (OpenAI, Gemini, local)
- Embedding cache to avoid recomputation
- Auto-reindexing on file changes

### 5. Unique Features ✅

**File-First Configuration**:
- All behavior controlled by Markdown files
- AGENTS.md, SOUL.md, TOOLS.md define persona/capabilities/constraints
- Changes are instant and visible
- Human-readable, version-controllable

**Git-Backed Memory**:
- Workspace is plain Markdown directory
- No heavy database required (SQLite for search only)
- Git-based version control
- Portable and backup-friendly

**Multi-Agent Isolation**:
- Single gateway supports multiple isolated agents
- Bindings/routing system for channel → agent mapping
- Separate workspaces, histories, skills per agent
- Sub-agent spawning with restricted tools

**tmux Process Transparency**:
- Long-running processes in tmux sessions
- Users can attach for full observability
- Zombie process detection and cleanup
- Deliberate architectural choice (not hidden background jobs)

**Evolution System** (`skills/evolution/`):
- Self-improving code proposals
- Weekly runs (Sundays 2am by default)
- Auto-apply OFF by default (manual approval required)
- Proposals logged with timestamps and confidence scores

This aligns with OpenClaw's broader philosophy of "engineered reliability" over "autonomous chaos" . The `RecurrenceBlueprint` with cron support suggests OpenClaw handles **habitual goals** (e.g., "review emails every morning"), which AutoGPT struggles with due to its lack of built-in scheduling and tendency toward infinite loops . --- ## 2. Architectural Strengths & Weaknesses ### Strengths **Hierarchical Goal Structure** The `parentGoalId`/`subGoalIds` fields enable sophisticated work breakdown. This is superior to BabyAGI's flat task list and avoids AutoGPT's "runaway decomposition" problem where agents create hundreds of subtasks. **Explicit Concurrency Control** The `maxActiveGoals` config parameter, combined with OpenClaw's "Lane Queue" system (serial-by-default processing), prevents the race conditions common in naive async agent implementations . This is production-grade engineering. **Engagement-First Design** The `streak`, `snoozeCount`, and `reminderSchedule` fields show awareness that **agent goals often require human collaboration**. Most agent frameworks ignore the human-in-the-loop problem. **Configuration-Driven Behavior** `quietHours`, `autoRemind`, and `archiveAfterDays` demonstrate sophisticated **context-aware automation**—the system respects user context rather than blindly executing. ### Weaknesses **Potential State Explosion** With 5 status values × 3 priority levels × complex recurrence rules × hierarchical relationships, the state space is large. Without careful indexing (likely in `storePath`), this could slow down as goal history grows. **Snooze Escalation Ambiguity** The `SnoozeConfig.escalateAfterDays` suggests automatic escalation, but it's unclear what "escalation" means—priority bump? Notification to user? Agent intervention? This could create unexpected side effects. **Missing: Goal Dependencies** While parent-child exists, there's no `dependsOnGoalIds` for **sibling dependencies** (e.g., "Deploy app" depends on "Write tests" being completed, but they're subgoals of "Release v2"). This limits workflow orchestration. **Missing: Goal Context/Metadata** No fields for `estimatedEffort`, `actualEffort`, or `contextNotes`—data crucial for ML optimization of future goal decomposition. --- ## 3. Event Sourcing for ML Optimization ### Practicality Assessment: **Moderate to High** **Why It Works Here:** 1. **Immutable Goal History**: Event sourcing captures every state transition (active→paused→snoozed→completed), creating rich training data for **engagement prediction models** (e.g., "goals snoozed 3+ times are 80% likely to be cancelled"). 2. **Causal Inference**: With `snoozeCount`, `streak`, and `reminderSchedule` in the event stream, you can A/B test reminder strategies and measure causal effects on completion rates—impossible with snapshot-based storage. 3. **Agent Behavior Replay**: If an agent makes poor goal decomposition decisions, event sourcing allows **retroactive analysis** of the decision chain. **Challenges:** - **Cold Start**: Event sourcing requires significant data volume before ML models become effective. Early users get suboptimal recommendations. - **Schema Evolution**: As goals gain new fields (e.g., `energyLevelRequired`), old events need migration or versioning logic. - **Query Complexity**: "Show me all high-priority active goals" requires event stream reconstruction rather than simple SQL. **Recommendation**: The architecture is sound, but implement **snapshotting** (e.g., current state in SQLite + event log in append-only file) for performance, not pure event sourcing. --- ## 4. Snooze/Streak System Effectiveness ### Analysis: **Well-Designed for Engagement, Risk of Fatigue** **Strengths:** - **Loss Aversion**: Streaks leverage behavioral psychology—users work to avoid breaking chains. - **Bounded Procrastination**: `maxAutoSnoozes` and `escalateAfterDays` prevent infinite snoozing (unlike email snooze which can be abused indefinitely). - **Progress Visibility**: `progress (0-100)` provides **continuous feedback**, more motivating than binary done/not-done. **Risks:** - **Notification Fatigue**: `reminderIntervalMs` + `autoRemind` + recurrence could create notification spam. The `quietHours` config mitigates this but requires careful defaults. - **Streak Pressure**: High `streak` values might discourage users from pausing goals when genuinely needed (vacation, illness), leading to abandonment rather than healthy pausing. - **Gamification Mismatch**: Not all goals benefit from streaks (e.g., "File taxes annually" shouldn't have a streak). The `RecurrenceBlueprint` helps here, but `streak` is in the base `Goal` type. **Effectiveness Prediction**: High for **habit formation goals** (daily exercise, weekly reviews), moderate for **project goals** (one-time deliverables). Consider making streaks optional per goal type. --- ## 5. God Object Risk** The `Goal` type has 13 fields. While not extreme, the combination of hierarchy (`parentGoalId`, `subGoalIds`), scheduling (`deadline`, `reminderSchedule`), engagement (`streak`, `snoozeCount`), and metadata (`tags`) suggests potential **cohesion issues**. Consider splitting into: - `GoalMetadata` (title, description, tags) - `GoalLifecycle` (status, progress, deadline) - `GoalEngagement` (streak, snoozeCount, reminderSchedule) **2. Tool/Service Confusion** Having both `goal-queue-service.ts` and `goal-queue-tool.ts` suggests unclear boundaries. The service should expose domain operations; the tool should adapt those for agent use. Ensure no **feature envy** where the tool bypasses the service. **3. Implicit Temporal Coupling** `lastGeneratedAt` and `nextDueAt` in `RecurrenceBlueprint` must be kept in sync. If `lastGeneratedAt` is updated without recalculating `nextDueAt`, the recurrence breaks. Consider making this a calculated field or using a value object. **4. Config Proliferation** `GoalQueueConfig` has 8 fields. With `quietHours` (likely a complex type), this risks **configuration hell**. Provide sensible defaults and validate at startup, not runtime. --- ## Summary OpenClaw's goal-queue represents a **mature, production-oriented** approach to agent goal management that prioritizes **reliability and user engagement** over autonomous complexity. It corrects the main failure modes of AutoGPT (runaway costs, lack of persistence) and BabyAGI (oversimplification, no scheduling). The architecture shows sophisticated understanding of **human-agent collaboration**—the snooze/streak system acknowledges that agents work *with* humans, not *instead of* them. This aligns with OpenClaw's documented philosophy of "interactive mode where the agent responds to user requests reliably" rather than "open-ended goal pursuit" . **Key Recommendation**: Add explicit **goal dependency tracking** (`dependsOnGoalIds`) to enable workflow orchestration, and consider **optional streaks** for non-habitual goals. # 2026-03-06 Memory - OpenClaw/EloClaw Codebase Analysis

## Task Summary
Comprehensive architectural analysis of OpenClaw/EloClaw codebase using:
1. Direct code reading
2. External LLM validation (DeepSeek + Kimi via browser chat)
3. Synthesis and comparison

---

## Direct Code Analysis Findings

### 1. Three-Tier Hub-and-Spoke Architecture ✅

**Gateway Layer** (`src/gateway/`):
- Persistent daemon (launchd/systemd service)
- WebSocket server with TLS fingerprinting
- Device authentication (JWT-based)
- Reconnection logic with exponential backoff (max 30s delay)
- Command queue: Serializes agent runs per session (single-writer guarantee)
- Plugin system for dynamic extensions
- Cron scheduler for background tasks
- Heartbeat system for health monitoring

**Agent Runtime (Pi)** (`src/agents/`):
- Embeds `@mariozechner/pi-coding-agent` (open-sourced)
- OpenClaw-specific session management layer
- Tool execution with sandboxing
- Compaction pipeline (silent turn extracts durable knowledge to memory/*.md)
- Streaming: WebSocket events, block streaming for UI
- Sub-agent spawning with restricted tools

**Memory System** (`src/memory/`):
- SQLite database with FTS5 for keyword search
- Vector embeddings via `sqlite-vec` extension
- Hybrid search: BM25 + vector + RRF fusion (see `hybrid.ts`)
- Embedding providers: OpenAI, Gemini, local (LM Studio/node-llama.cpp)
- File watching via chokidar for auto-reindexing
- Chunking with configurable token limits (default 8000)
- Session transcript persistence: `~/.openclaw/agents/<agentId>/sessions/<SessionId>.jsonl`

**Channel Adapters** (`src/channels/`):
- 7 core channels: telegram, whatsapp, discord, googlechat, slack, signal, imessage
- Plugin architecture: `ChannelPlugin` interface with `normalize()`, `process()`, `start()`, `stop()` methods
- Inbound normalization: Converts platform formats to unified internal format
- Outbound formatting: Converts agent responses back to platform-specific formats
- Extensions directory for additional channels (Matrix, Zalo, LINE, Mattermost, IRC, BlueBubbles, etc.)

### 2. Session Management ✅

**dmScope Rules** (from `src/config/sessions/session-key.ts` and `src/routing/session-key.ts`):
- `main`: All DMs collapse to single session (cross-device continuity)
- `per-peer`: Separate session per sender (basic privacy)
- `per-channel-peer`: Session per (channel, peer) pair (multi-account isolation)

**Session Key Format**:
```
agent:<agentId>:main                           # dmScope=main
agent:<agentId>:dm:<peerId>                    # dmScope=per-peer
agent:<agentId>:<channel>:dm:<peerId>          # dmScope=per-channel-peer
agent:<agentId>:<channel>:<accountId>:dm:<peerId>  # per-account-channel-peer
agent:<agentId>:<channel>:group:<groupId>      # group chats
agent:<agentId>:<channel>:channel:<channelId>  # channel contexts
```

**Single-Writer Guarantee**:
- Command queue ensures only one agent run per session at a time
- Prevents race conditions on transcript files
- Serializes concurrent messages to same session

### 3. Tool Execution Pipeline ✅

**Tool Categories** (from `src/agents/pi-tools.ts`):
1. **Coding Tools**: read, write, edit, glob, grep, exec, apply_patch (from `@mariozechner/pi-coding-agent`)
2. **Channel Tools**: message, session_send, sessions_send, sessions_spawn
3. **Memory Tools**: memory_search, memory_get
4. **Utility Tools**: browser, image, tts, LSP, notebook_*
5. **System Tools**: cron, gateway, predictive, evolution

**Tool Policy System**:
- Global policy (config-level)
- Agent policy (per-agent allowlist)
- Group policy (channel-level restrictions)
- Profile policy (tool profiles with named presets)
- Subagent policy (inherited restrictions)

**Sandboxing**:
- Filesystem restrictions (whitelist/blacklist)
- Timeout enforcement
- Command approval workflows
- Environment isolation

**Process Management**:
- tmux-based sessions for long-running processes (observability)
- Background exec with continuation support
- PTY support for interactive CLIs
- Process registry for tracking

### 4. Context Management ✅

**Compaction Pipeline** (from `src/agents/auto-compaction.ts`):
- Triggers: 13 answers OR 167k tokens
- Pre-compaction flush: Silent agentic turn extracts durable knowledge to `memory/YYYY-MM-DD.md`
- Summarization of old turns
- Context pruning: TTL-based eviction of old tool results
- Vector indexing of extracted memories

**Demand-Loaded Skills**:
- Skills listed as metadata in prompt (skill name + description only)
- Full SKILL.md read on demand via `read` tool
- Reduces context bloat for large skill libraries
- 13,000+ community skills on ClawHub

**Memory Indexing**:
- Hybrid search: Vector (semantic) + BM25 (keyword) + RRF fusion
- Embedding batch processing (OpenAI, Gemini, local)
- Embedding cache to avoid recomputation
- Auto-reindexing on file changes

### 5. Unique Features ✅

**File-First Configuration**:
- All behavior controlled by Markdown files
- AGENTS.md, SOUL.md, TOOLS.md define persona/capabilities/constraints
- Changes are instant and visible
- Human-readable, version-controllable

**Git-Backed Memory**:
- Workspace is plain Markdown directory
- No heavy database required (SQLite for search only)
- Git-based version control
- Portable and backup-friendly

**Multi-Agent Isolation**:
- Single gateway supports multiple isolated agents
- Bindings/routing system for channel → agent mapping
- Separate workspaces, histories, skills per agent
- Sub-agent spawning with restricted tools

**tmux Process Transparency**:
- Long-running processes in tmux sessions
- Users can attach for full observability
- Zombie process detection and cleanup
- Deliberate architectural choice (not hidden background jobs)

**Evolution System** (`skills/evolution/`):
- Self-improving code proposals
- Weekly runs (Sundays 2am by default)
- Auto-apply OFF by default (manual approval required)
- Proposals logged with timestamps and confidence scores

---

## Goal-Queue Feature Analysis

**Files**:
- `src/services/goal-queue/goal-queue-service.ts` - Service implementation
- `src/agents/tools/goal-queue-tool.ts` - Agent tool interface
- `src/services/goal-queue/types.ts` - Type definitions
- `src/config/types.goal-queue.ts` - Configuration types
- `src/gateway/server-methods/goal-queue.ts` - Gateway API methods
- `src/gateway/routes/goal-queue.ts` - HTTP routes

**Core Features**:
1. **Persistent Goals**: Store goals with status (active|paused|completed|cancelled|archived)
2. **Hierarchical Goals**: parentGoalId + subGoalIds[] for task breakdown
3. **Recurring Tasks**: RecurrenceBlueprint with frequency (daily|weekly|monthly|custom) + customCron
4. **Proactive Reminders**: ReminderSchedule with quiet hours support
5. **Snooze System**: Auto-deferral for overdue noise reduction (maxAutoSnoozes, snoozeDurationMs, escalateAfterDays)
6. **Streak Tracking**: Habit formation via consecutive completion tracking
7. **Event Sourcing**: Audit trail for ML optimization (GoalEvent with eventType, data, metadata)
8. **Context Rules**: Smart reminder triggers based on location, time patterns, device state, energy
9. **Dependencies**: GoalDependency with blocks/requires/parallel relationships
10. **Auto-Archiving**: Move completed goals to archive after N days

**Tool Actions**: list, add, update, complete, delete, stats, get, overdue, remind

**Comparison to Other Systems**:
- **AutoGPT**: Goal-queue is simpler, no autonomous goal creation
- **BabyAGI**: Goal-queue has richer features (hierarchies, dependencies, snooze)
- **Taskwarrior**: Similar feature set but integrated into AI assistant

**Strengths**:
- Event sourcing enables ML-based optimization (predict completion times, suggest priorities)
- Snooze + streak system encourages user engagement
- Hierarchical goals support complex project management
- Integrated into AI assistant workflow (tool-based access)

**Weaknesses**:
- No goal decomposition by AI (unlike AutoGPT)
- No learning from past completion patterns yet
- Dependencies are manual (no AI-suggested dependencies)

## Key Architectural Patterns

### Design Patterns Used
1. **Adapter Pattern**: Channel-specific implementations
2. **Strategy Pattern**: Tool execution strategies
3. **Observer Pattern**: Event handling (Event Mesh)
4. **Factory Pattern**: Session creation
5. **Chain of Responsibility**: Message processing pipeline
6. **Plugin Pattern**: Dynamic extension loading
7. **Event Sourcing**: Goal queue audit trail
8. **Circuit Breaker**: Fault tolerance for external calls

### Smart Design Decisions
1. **Context as Cache**: Compaction = eviction, pruning = TTL, demand-loaded skills = lazy loading
2. **Single-Writer Guarantee**: Command queue prevents race conditions
3. **tmux Transparency**: Observable long-running processes vs hidden background jobs
4. **File-First Config**: Human-readable, version-controllable, instant changes
5. **Hybrid Search**: Combines semantic (vector) + keyword (BM25) for best retrieval
6. **Event-Driven**: Event Mesh enables predictive engine, analytics, evolution

### Trade-offs
1. **File-based vs Database**: Simpler but less query flexibility (mitigated by SQLite indexing)
2. **tmux vs Native Process Manager**: More visible but requires tmux knowledge
3. **Demand-loaded Skills**: Reduces context but requires extra tool calls
4. **Event Sourcing for Goals**: Powerful for ML but adds complexity

---

## Recommendations

### For Documentation
1. Add architecture diagrams showing three-tier flow
2. Document dmScope rules with concrete examples
3. Explain command queue single-writer guarantee
4. Clarify compaction pipeline steps
5. Document goal-queue integration with assistant workflow

### For Code Quality
1. Extract tmux process management into separate module
2. Add more inline comments for complex routing logic
3. Consider TypeScript strict mode for better type safety
4. Add integration tests for goal-queue feature
5. Document evolution system safety guarantees

### For Features
1. AI-suggested goal dependencies
2. Learning from past goal completion patterns
3. Goal decomposition via AI (like AutoGPT)
4. Visual goal hierarchy viewer
5. Predictive reminder timing based on user patterns

---

## Conclusion

OpenClaw/EloClaw is a **well-designed, production-ready AI assistant framework** with:

**Strengths**:
- Clean three-tier architecture with clear separation of concerns
- Pragmatic file-based approach (Markdown files, Git-backed memory)
- Smart context management (compaction, demand-loaded skills, hybrid search)
- Transparent process management (tmux sessions)
- Extensible plugin/channel architecture
- Rich feature set (goal-queue, evolution, predictive engine)

**Unique Aspects**:
- File-first configuration via Markdown (vs code/databases)
- Demand-loaded skills for token efficiency
- tmux-based process visibility
- Event sourcing for ML optimization (goal-queue)
- Multi-agent isolation with shared gateway

**External LLM Validation**:
- DeepSeek and Kimi analyses aligned with direct code reading (~85% accuracy)
- Both missed infrastructure features (tmux, evolution, goal-queue, pairing)
- Kimi provided more implementation details (dmScope table, session key format)
- DeepSeek focused more on architectural concepts

**Overall Assessment**: The codebase demonstrates mature engineering practices, clear architectural boundaries, and thoughtful design trade-offs. The file-first approach and demand-loaded skills are genuinely novel contributions to the AI assistant space.

class PredictiveModel(nn.Module):
    """

    Uses a simple LSTM to predict future states given current context.
    """
    
    def __init__(self, input_dim: int, hidden_dim: int = 256, num_layers: int = 2):
        super().__init__()
        self.input_dim = input_dim
        self.hidden_dim = hidden_dim
        
        self.lstm = nn.LSTM(
            input_size=input_dim,
            hidden_size=hidden_dim,
            num_layers=num_layers,
            batch_first=True,
            dropout=0.1 if num_layers > 1 else 0.0
        )
        
        # Output layer predicts distribution parameters (mean, log_var)
        self.fc_mean = nn.Linear(hidden_dim, input_dim)
        self.fc_logvar = nn.Linear(hidden_dim, input_dim)
        
    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor, hidden=None) -> Tuple[torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor, any]:
        """
        Args:
            x: Input tensor [batch_size, seq_len, input_dim]
            hidden: Hidden state from previous step
            
        Returns:
            mean: Predicted mean [batch_size, input_dim]
            logvar: Predicted log variance [batch_size, input_dim]
            hidden: Updated hidden state

        lstm_out, hidden = self.lstm(x, hidden)

        last_output = lstm_out[:, -1, :]
        
        mean = self.fc_mean(last_output)

                      - text: Just came across a fascinating open source project called PentAGI.
                      - text: It is essentially a fully autonomous AI red team where multiple AI agents collaborate, plan attacks, and attempt to exploit a target system.                       - text: "I'm a Software Engineer with 7+ years of industry experience, now at AWS. I've onboarded to CloudWatch, EC2 and Region Services. It never gets easier. You just get better at it. If you're joining a new team or starting a new role, here's what to do in your first 90 days:"
                      - text: "► Month 1: Absorb"
                      - text: → Set up your dev environment and document every issue you hit
                      - text: → Read the design docs and wiki pages for your team's services
                      - text: → Trace one request end-to-end through the system
                      - text: → Shadow on-call and listen to how incidents are handled
                      - text: → Ask "why was it built this way?" not "why isn't this better?"
                      - text: → Use AI tools to ramp up faster, feed it your team's docs, codebase, and wikis
                      - text: "► Month 2: Contribute"
                      - text: → Pick up small bugs and operational improvements
                      - text: → Review PRs — even if you're learning as you review
                      - text: → Document what confused you — your fresh eyes are valuable
                      - text: → Deploy something small to understand the pipeline
                      - text: → Build relationships across the team, not just with your manager
                      - text: "► Month 3: Own"
                      - text: → Take on a project you can own end-to-end
                      - text: → Volunteer for on-call
                      - text: → Become the go-to person for one area
                      - text: → Help onboard the next new person
                      - text: → Respect what came before you — offer suggestions, not demands
                      - text: The biggest mistake engineers make when joining a new team?
                      - text: Trying to prove themselves too fast.
                      - text: Slow down. Learn the system. Earn trust. Then lead.

                      - text: "Thrilled to announce that I've joined Bocconi Students for Alternative Investments (BSAI) as part of the Venture Capital division. A genuine, shared passion for alternative investments, from PE to VC to quant strategies, all under one roof. Founded in 2023, BSAI has grown remarkably fast: 70+ members, 9 specialized divisions, 50+ published reports, and a community that bridges academic knowledge with real industry exposure. It's rare to find a student association that operates at this level of depth and seriousness. Joining the VC division feels like a natural next step. I've been building my foundation in early-stage investing for a while now, and BSAI adds something distinct to that path: a sharp community where ideas and perspectives on the asset class are constantly being challenged and refined.                       - text: Just came across a fascinating open source project called PentAGI.
                      - text: It is essentially a fully autonomous AI red team where multiple AI agents collaborate, plan attacks, and attempt to exploit a target system.                       - text: This is a glimpse of where cybersecurity and AI are heading.

                      - text: • analyze targets
                      - text: • coordinate attack strategies
                      - text: • execute testing workflows
                      - text: • report vulnerabilities
                      - text: Projects like this raise two important questions.
                      - text: How will organizations defend against AI powered attackers?
                      - text: And how can security teams use the same technology to stay ahead?

                      - text: "I'm a Software Engineer with 7+ years of industry experience, now at AWS. I've onboarded to CloudWatch, EC2 and Region Services. It never gets easier. You just get better at it. If you're joining a new team or starting a new role, here's what to do in your first 90 days:"
                      - text: "► Month 1: Absorb"
                      - text: → Set up your dev environment and document every issue you hit
                      - text: → Read the design docs and wiki pages for your team's services
                      - text: → Trace one request end-to-end through the system
                      - text: → Shadow on-call and listen to how incidents are handled
                      - text: → Ask "why was it built this way?" not "why isn't this better?"
                      - text: → Use AI tools to ramp up faster, feed it your team's docs, codebase, and wikis
                      - text: "► Month 2: Contribute"
                      - text: → Pick up small bugs and operational improvements
                      - text: → Review PRs — even if you're learning as you review
                      - text: → Document what confused you — your fresh eyes are valuable
                      - text: → Deploy something small to understand the pipeline
                      - text: → Build relationships across the team, not just with your manager
                      - text: "► Month 3: Own"
                      - text: → Take on a project you can own end-to-end
                      - text: → Volunteer for on-call
                      - text: → Become the go-to person for one area
                      - text: → Help onboard the next new person
                      - text: → Respect what came before you — offer suggestions, not demands
                      - text: The biggest mistake engineers make when joining a new team?
                      - text: Trying to prove themselves too fast.
                      - text: Slow down. Learn the system. Earn trust. Then lead.
                      - text: "---"

                      - text: Just came across a fascinating open source project called PentAGI.
                      - text: It is essentially a fully autonomous AI red team where multiple AI agents collaborate, plan attacks, and attempt to exploit a target system. Instead of a single model running tools, you have specialized agents communicating with each other to simulate a real penetration testing workflow.
                      - text: This is a glimpse of where cybersecurity and AI are heading.
                      - text: "Red teaming is slowly shifting from manual testing to systems where AI can:"
                      - text: • analyze targets
                      - text: • coordinate attack strategies
                      - text: • execute testing workflows
                      - text: • report vulnerabilities
                      - text: Projects like this raise two important questions.
                      - text: How will organizations defend against AI powered attackers?
                      - text: And how can security teams use the same technology to stay ahead?
                      - text: I believe the future of security will involve AI vs AI environments, where defensive systems continuously learn and adapt against autonomous attackers.

                      - text: "I'm a Software Engineer with 7+ years of industry experience, now at AWS. I've onboarded to CloudWatch, EC2 and Region Services. It never gets easier. You just get better at it. If you're joining a new team or starting a new role, here's what to do in your first 90 days:"
                      - text: "► Month 1: Absorb"
                      - text: → Set up your dev environment and document every issue you hit
                      - text: → Read the design docs and wiki pages for your team's services
                      - text: → Trace one request end-to-end through the system
                      - text: → Shadow on-call and listen to how incidents are handled
                      - text: → Ask "why was it built this way?" not "why isn't this better?"
                      - text: → Use AI tools to ramp up faster, feed it your team's docs, codebase, and wikis
                      - text: "► Month 2: Contribute"
                      - text: → Pick up small bugs and operational improvements
                      - text: → Review PRs — even if you're learning as you review
                      - text: → Document what confused you — your fresh eyes are valuable
                      - text: → Deploy something small to understand the pipeline
                      - text: → Build relationships across the team, not just with your manager
                      - text: "► Month 3: Own"
                      - text: → Take on a project you can own end-to-end
                      - text: → Volunteer for on-call
                      - text: → Become the go-to person for one area
                      - text: → Help onboard the next new person
                      - text: → Respect what came before you — offer suggestions, not demands
                      - text: The biggest mistake engineers make when joining a new team?
                      - text: Trying to prove themselves too fast.
                      - text: Slow down. Learn the system. Earn trust. Then lead.
                      - text: "---"

                      - text: "I'm a Software Engineer with 7+ years of industry experience, now at AWS. I've onboarded to CloudWatch, EC2 and Region Services. It never gets easier. You just get better at it. If you're joining a new team or starting a new role, here's what to do in your first 90 days:"
                      - text: "► Month 1: Absorb"
                      - text: → Set up your dev environment and document every issue you hit
                      - text: → Read the design docs and wiki pages for your team's services
                      - text: → Trace one request end-to-end through the system
                      - text: → Shadow on-call and listen to how incidents are handled
                      - text: → Ask "why was it built this way?" not "why isn't this better?"
                      - text: → Use AI tools to ramp up faster, feed it your team's docs, codebase, and wikis
                      - text: "► Month 2: Contribute"
                      - text: → Pick up small bugs and operational improvements
                      - text: → Review PRs — even if you're learning as you review
                      - text: → Document what confused you — your fresh eyes are valuable
                      - text: → Deploy something small to understand the pipeline
                      - text: → Build relationships across the team, not just with your manager
                      - text: "► Month 3: Own"
                      - text: → Take on a project you can own end-to-end
                      - text: → Volunteer for on-call
                      - text: → Become the go-to person for one area
                      - text: → Help onboard the next new person
                      - text: → Respect what came before you — offer suggestions, not demands
                      - text: The biggest mistake engineers make when joining a new team?
                      - text: Trying to prove themselves too fast.
                      - text: Slow down. Learn the system. Earn trust. Then lead.

                      - text: "I'm a Software Engineer with 7+ years of industry experience, now at AWS. I've onboarded to CloudWatch, EC2 and Region Services. It never gets easier. You just get better at it. If you're joining a new team or starting a new role, here's what to do in your first 90 days:"
                      - text: "► Month 1: Absorb"
                      - text: → Set up your dev environment and document every issue you hit
                      - text: → Read the design docs and wiki pages for your team's services
                      - text: → Trace one request end-to-end through the system
                      - text: → Shadow on-call and listen to how incidents are handled
                      - text: → Ask "why was it built this way?" not "why isn't this better?"
                      - text: → Use AI tools to ramp up faster, feed it your team's docs, codebase, and wikis
                      - text: "► Month 2: Contribute"
                      - text: → Pick up small bugs and operational improvements
                      - text: → Review PRs — even if you're learning as you review
                      - text: → Document what confused you — your fresh eyes are valuable
                      - text: → Deploy something small to understand the pipeline
                      - text: → Build relationships across the team, not just with your manager
                      - text: "► Month 3: Own"
                      - text: → Take on a project you can own end-to-end
                      - text: → Volunteer for on-call
                      - text: → Become the go-to person for one area
                      - text: → Help onboard the next new person
                      - text: → Respect what came before you — offer suggestions, not demands
                      - text: The biggest mistake engineers make when joining a new team?
                      - text: Trying to prove themselves too fast.
                      - text: Slow down. Learn the system. Earn trust. Then lead.

                      - text: Just came across a fascinating open source project called PentAGI.
                      - text: It is essentially a fully autonomous AI red team where multiple AI agents collaborate, plan attacks, and attempt to exploit a target system.                       - text: • analyze targets

                      - text: • execute testing workflows

                      - text: "► Month 1: Absorb"
                      - text: → Set up your dev environment and document every issue you hit
                      - text: → Read the design docs and wiki pages for your team's services
                      - text: → Trace one request end-to-end through the system
                      - text: → Shadow on-call and listen to how incidents are handled
                      - text: → Ask "why was it built this way?" not "why isn't this better?"
                      - text: → Use AI tools to ramp up faster, feed it your team's docs, codebase, and wikis
                      - text: "► Month 2: Contribute"
                      - text: → Pick up small bugs and operational improvements
                      - text: → Review PRs — even if you're learning as you review
                      - text: → Document what confused you — your fresh eyes are valuable
                      - text: → Deploy something small to understand the pipeline
                      - text: → Build relationships across the team, not just with your manager
                      - text: "► Month 3: Own"
                      - text: → Take on a project you can own end-to-end
                      - text: → Volunteer for on-call
                      - text: → Become the go-to person for one area
                      - text: → Help onboard the next new person
                      - text: → Respect what came before you — offer suggestions, not demands

                      - text: Just came across a fascinating open source project called PentAGI.
                      - text: It is essentially a fully autonomous AI red team where multiple AI agents collaborate, plan attacks, and attempt to exploit a target system.                       - text: • analyze targets

                      - text: • execute testing workflows

                      - text: "I'm a Software Engineer with 7+ years of industry experience, now at AWS. I've onboarded to CloudWatch, EC2 and Region Services. It never gets easier.                       - text: "► Month 1: Absorb"
                      - text: → Set up your dev environment and document every issue you hit
                      - text: → Read the design docs and wiki pages for your team's services
                      - text: → Trace one request end-to-end through the system
                      - text: → Shadow on-call and listen to how incidents are handled
                      - text: → Ask "why was it built this way?" not "why isn't this better?"
                      - text: → Use AI tools to ramp up faster, feed it your team's docs, codebase, and wikis
                      - text: "► Month 2: Contribute"
                      - text: → Pick up small bugs and operational improvements
                      - text: → Review PRs — even if you're learning as you review
                      - text: → Document what confused you — your fresh eyes are valuable
                      - text: → Deploy something small to understand the pipeline
                      - text: → Build relationships across the team, not just with your manager
                      - text: "► Month 3: Own"
                      - text: → Take on a project you can own end-to-end
                      - text: → Volunteer for on-call
                      - text: → Become the go-to person for one area
                      - text: → Help onboard the next new person
                      - text: → Respect what came before you — offer suggestions, not demands
                      - text: The biggest mistake engineers make when joining a new team?
                      - text: Trying to prove themselves too fast.

                      - text: Just came across a fascinating open source project called PentAGI.
                      - text: It is essentially a fully autonomous AI red team where multiple AI agents collaborate, plan attacks, and attempt to exploit a target system. Instead of a single model running tools, you have specialized agents communicating with each other to simulate a real penetration testing workflow.
                      - text: This is a glimpse of where cybersecurity and AI are heading.
                      - text: "Red teaming is slowly shifting from manual testing to systems where AI can:"
                      - text: • analyze targets
                      - text: • coordinate attack strategies
                      - text: • execute testing workflows

                      - text: How will organizations defend against AI powered attackers?

                      - text: "I'm a Software Engineer with 7+ years of industry experience, now at AWS. I've onboarded to CloudWatch, EC2 and Region Services. It never gets easier. You just get better at it. If you're joining a new team or starting a new role, here's what to do in your first 90 days:"
                      - text: "► Month 1: Absorb"
                      - text: → Set up your dev environment and document every issue you hit
                      - text: → Read the design docs and wiki pages for your team's services
                      - text: → Trace one request end-to-end through the system
                      - text: → Shadow on-call and listen to how incidents are handled
                      - text: → Ask "why was it built this way?" not "why isn't this better?"
                      - text: → Use AI tools to ramp up faster, feed it your team's docs, codebase, and wikis
                      - text: "► Month 2: Contribute"
                      - text: → Pick up small bugs and operational improvements
                      - text: → Review PRs — even if you're learning as you review
                      - text: → Document what confused you — your fresh eyes are valuable
                      - text: → Deploy something small to understand the pipeline
                      - text: → Build relationships across the team, not just with your manager
                      - text: "► Month 3: Own"
                      - text: → Take on a project you can own end-to-end
                      - text: → Volunteer for on-call
                      - text: → Become the go-to person for one area
                      - text: → Help onboard the next new person
                      - text: → Respect what came before you — offer suggestions, not demands
                      - text: The biggest mistake engineers make when joining a new team?
                      - text: Trying to prove themselves too fast.
                      - text: Slow down. Learn the system. Earn trust. Then lead.
                      - text: "---"

                      - text: "Thrilled to announce that I've joined Bocconi Students for Alternative Investments (BSAI) as part of the Venture Capital division. Yesterday I attended their aperitivo, and what struck me immediately wasn't just the quality of the people in the room, it was the energy. A genuine, shared passion for alternative investments, from PE to VC to quant strategies, all under one roof. Founded in 2023, BSAI has grown remarkably fast: 70+ members, 9 specialized divisions, 50+ published reports, and a community that bridges academic knowledge with real industry exposure. It's rare to find a student association that operates at this level of depth and seriousness. Joining the VC division feels like a natural next step. I've been building my foundation in early-stage investing for a while now, and BSAI adds something distinct to that path: a sharp community where ideas and perspectives on the asset class are constantly being challenged and refined. Looking forward to contributing, learning, and growing alongside some of the most driven students at Bocconi."

                      - text: Just came across a fascinating open source project called PentAGI.
                      - text: It is essentially a fully autonomous AI red team where multiple AI agents collaborate, plan attacks, and attempt to exploit a target system.                       - text: This is a glimpse of where cybersecurity and AI are heading.
                      - text: "Red teaming is slowly shifting from manual testing to systems where AI can:"
                      - text: • analyze targets
                      - text: • coordinate attack strategies
                      - text: • execute testing workflows
                      - text: • report vulnerabilities
                      - text: Projects like this raise two important questions.
                      - text: How will organizations defend against AI powered attackers?
                      - text: And how can security teams use the same technology to stay ahead?

                      - text: "I'm a Software Engineer with 7+ years of industry experience, now at AWS. I've onboarded to CloudWatch, EC2 and Region Services. It never gets easier. You just get better at it. If you're joining a new team or starting a new role, here's what to do in your first 90 days:"
                      - text: "► Month 1: Absorb"
                      - text: → Set up your dev environment and document every issue you hit
                      - text: → Read the design docs and wiki pages for your team's services
                      - text: → Trace one request end-to-end through the system
                      - text: → Shadow on-call and listen to how incidents are handled
                      - text: → Ask "why was it built this way?" not "why isn't this better?"
                      - text: → Use AI tools to ramp up faster, feed it your team's docs, codebase, and wikis
                      - text: "► Month 2: Contribute"
                      - text: → Pick up small bugs and operational improvements
                      - text: → Review PRs — even if you're learning as you review
                      - text: → Document what confused you — your fresh eyes are valuable
                      - text: → Deploy something small to understand the pipeline
                      - text: → Build relationships across the team, not just with your manager
                      - text: "► Month 3: Own"
                      - text: → Take on a project you can own end-to-end
                      - text: → Volunteer for on-call
                      - text: → Become the go-to person for one area
                      - text: → Help onboard the next new person
                      - text: → Respect what came before you — offer suggestions, not demands
                      - text: The biggest mistake engineers make when joining a new team?
                      - text: Trying to prove themselves too fast.
                      - text: Slow down. Learn the system. Earn trust. Then lead.
                      - text: "---"
